The transfer holds for `fact` and is weaker for `claim`, which is the verb the design turns on by default.

`scope.rs`'s construction has two properties, and C1 carries only one across. The extent is (i) not typeable — "deliberately no flag to type one in" — and (ii) COMPLETE: `look` and `run` "record what they actually opened", so the author cannot exclude part of it either. Both together are what make the comparison unfakeable by one hand.

For a claim, property (i) survives — the author cannot type the cited facts' captured output. Property (ii) does not. The captured side of the comparison is the output of the facts the author CHOSE to cite, and that choice is entirely author-controlled. tetel already treats it as unreliable: the `claim` tool description in src/mcp.rs:689 exists to warn about it — creating a claim "returns an OVERLAP REPORT: the id and shared designator(s) ... of every other fact whose extent touches the same file or command as the facts you cited, and which you did NOT cite ... read it and decide whether one of them belongs in this claim". An author with an overreaching proposition can cite only the facts consistent with it and the semantic verifier sees no disagreement — not because the sides agree, but because the disagreeing side was filtered out before the comparison. That is the author's diligence doing the work, which is precisely what C1's last sentence denies.

This is a `qualifies` and not a refutation: the construction still beats the abandoned `Domain ⊆ Extent`, where the author typed the domain outright. But the design should say which facts the comparison sees. If it is only `cites`, the independence claim must be narrowed to "cannot be made vacuous by typing, but can be narrowed by selection". If instead the comparison ran against the cited facts UNION the overlap set — facts already computed, already on disk, already surfaced at claim time — property (ii) would be restored and the transfer would be intact. That is a design choice this memo does not make.
